Definition: Whether procedural rules for collection, storage, and sharing of ID-related personal data are publicly available and established
Comments: Data sharing rules exist but are only partially defined. The ROPA 2015 (Section 65) specifies permitted uses of NIR data (security, taxation, health, social services, immigration etc.) and NIRA controls TPI access for third parties. The Data Protection and Privacy Act 2019 sets consent and purpose-limitation rules for data sharing. However, civil society has raised concerns about inadequate safeguards and opaque data sharing with security agencies.

Definition: Whether specific regulation or policy addresses digital ID beyond general identification legislation
Comments: The Registration of Persons Act 2015 is a dedicated legal instrument specifically governing Uganda's digital/biometric national ID system, establishing NIRA, the NIR, biometric enrollment requirements, mandatory card use, and data management rules. This constitutes digital ID-specific regulation beyond general e-government law.

Definition: Whether national data protection legislation exists and covers personal data linked to the ID system
Comments: Uganda enacted the Data Protection and Privacy Act (DPPA) No. 9 of 2019, which regulates the collection, processing, and use of personal data including biometric data in the national ID system. The Act establishes seven data protection principles, data subject rights (access, rectification, erasure), consent requirements, and breach notification obligations.

Definition: Whether a Data Protection Authority or similar body regulates ID data collection and sharing by the ID system
Comments: Uganda's Data Protection and Privacy Act 2019 establishes the Personal Data Protection Office (PDPO) under NITA-U, headed by a National Personal Data Protection Director. The PDPO is mandated to enforce the DPPA, investigate complaints, conduct audits, maintain a data protection register, and supervise data collectors and processors. The PDPO recorded its first-ever criminal conviction under the DPPA in July 2025.

Definition: Whether the digital ID credential serves as legal proof of an individual's identity as codified in law
Comments: Under Section 69 of the Registration of Persons Act 2015, the national identification card is prima facie proof of the particulars contained in it, including citizenship. The NIN serves as legal proof of identity for accessing services including banking, SIM registration, health, education, elections, and property transactions. The High Court upheld the legality of using the NID as the primary identification instrument.

Definition: Whether formal legislation (act, law, regulation) governs digital identity including identification acts, digital ID laws, or equivalent legislation
Comments: Uganda has a comprehensive legal framework for its national ID system. The Registration of Persons Act (ROPA) 2015 (Cap. 332) establishes NIRA, the NIR, and mandates compulsory registration of citizens and alien residents. It sets out data use, mandatory use of national ID cards for services (Section 66), and offences. The system was originally launched under the National Security Information System (NSIS) in 2014.

Definition: Whether the digital ID is recognized or interoperable across borders through regional agreements or travel documents
Value Name: Recognized in some regional contexts (e.g., ECOWAS travel)
Comments: Uganda's national ID is formally recognised as a travel document for cross-border movement within the East African Community (EAC), specifically between Uganda, Kenya, and Rwanda under the Northern Corridor Integration Projects (NCIP) agreement from January 2014. Citizens of these three countries can cross each other's borders using national IDs in lieu of passports. Tanzania does not participate as it lacks a national ID system. This constitutes formal regional interoperability among some EAC states.

Definition: Whether registration for digital ID is mandatory, optional, or mandatory for specific groups
Comments: Registration is compulsory for all citizens and legal alien residents under Part VIII of the Registration of Persons Act 2015 (Section 54: 'Compulsory registration'). The NID is mandatory for accessing a wide range of services including SIM registration, banking, health, education, social services, passports, and voter registration. The High Court in June 2025 upheld the mandatory use of NID for accessing services.

Definition: Whether credential is accepted or mandatory for accessing public healthcare services
Comments: The national ID is mandatory for accessing healthcare in Uganda. Pregnant women without NID have been turned away from health centres; citizens without NID are denied access to National Health System services. CIPESA (2023) and civil society organisations documented unregistered individuals being denied healthcare. The mandatory NID requirement was challenged in the High Court by ISER and others, but upheld in June 2025.

Definition: Whether non-nationals including refugees, asylum seekers, and permanent residents are eligible to register
Comments: Legal alien residents (with valid permits/passes under the Uganda Citizenship and Immigration Control Act) are eligible for Alien Identification Numbers (AIN) and Alien ID cards under ROPA 2015 (Sections 72–74). However, refugees recognised by the government and UNHCR are explicitly excluded from ROPA (Section 1(2)(b)) and are managed separately by the Office of the Prime Minister. Thus only some non-nationals (legal residents but not refugees) are eligible.

Definition: Whether credential is accepted or mandatory for SIM card activation and mobile service registration
Comments: SIM card registration requiring a national ID is mandatory in Uganda. The Registration of Persons Act 2015 (Section 66) mandated NID for SIM card registration. This was enforced starting 2017, with all five mobile network operators (MNOs) connected to NIRA's TPI for biometric SIM verification. Citizens without an NID cannot register a SIM card. CIPESA and Yale Law School have documented this mandatory requirement and its exclusionary effects.
